newsitem.title: USA: US banks, credit unions offer little common ground.
newsitem.headline: US banks, credit unions offer little common ground.

text.p: Legislators seeking to resolve the dispute between banks and credit unions heard from both industries on Wednesday but neither side backed down from long-held positions.

Banks urged members of the House Banking Committee's financial institutions subcommittee to limit credit union membership and impose federal taxes on the non-profit cooperatives. Credit unions asked for looser membership rules.
Subcommittee chairwoman Marge Roukema said after the hearing she heard little willingness to compromise, but said it was still early in the process.
Wednesday's hearing was Congress's first on the membership issue. The two industries are also battling in court, with the Supreme Court to hear the case in the fall.
"It may be unrealistic to think that we could (find common ground) at this point in time, but I'm certainly willing to try," Roukema, Republican of New Jersey, told reporters.

Credit union executives, in town for an industry gathering, descended on Capitol Hill in droves on Tuesday to make their case. Legislators seemed eager to voice general support for credit unions, without endorsing either side's position in the membership controversy.
The subcommittee hearing was well-attended, with at least 16 members, including full committee chairman Jim Leach, spending time listening to testimony.

"I know there is intense interest, certainly because (members of Congress) have been hearing a lot from their credit unions and their banks back home," Roukema said. "They are both grass roots constituencies and we've got their attention."
Many of the legislators tried to prompt the witnesses for compromise approaches, but few new ideas were forthcoming.

"There are no guarantees that anything can be resolved but there are going to be totally open minds," chairman Leach said during the hearing. "We're going to try and move towards consensus if at all possible."
"We expect to give both sides the fairest possible hearing and we will be open to any and all reasonable suggestions," the Iowa Republican added.
Ranking subcomittee Democrat Bruce Vento of Minnesota urged Congress to maintain a vibrant credit unions industry.
"I intend to work to keep the credit unions and the credit union movement relevent in financial services and in serving my constituents today and in the future," Vento said.
Created by a 1934 act of Congress, credit unions typically comprised members of a distinct group, such as people who worked for the same employer or lived in the same neighborhood.

But, in 1982, with the an economic downturn threatening many financial institutions, the federal regulator of the industry decided to allow credit unions to diversify by signing up members of more than one group.
In 1990, banks sued one such multi-group credit union, AT&T Family Federal Credit Union in North Carolina, which had grown to encompass over 150 groups.
Last July an appeals court sided with the banks, holding that credit unions should be limited to members with a single "common bond."
The ruling, if upheld, will lead to the "long-term erosion of certain credit unions," said Michael Vadala, presdient of the Summit Federal Credit Union of Rochester, New York.

By contrast, Scott Jones, first vice president of the American Bankers Association, said credit unions needed to be curbed. "Taxpayer dollars are already subsidizing people who can afford unsubsidized financial services," he said.
--Aaron Pressman((202-898-8312))
